title: The Threshold, Not the Model: A Cost-Sensitive Re-Evaluation of Offensive Language Detection on the Offensive Language Identification Dataset (OLID)
abstract: Offensive language detection benchmarks, including the widely used OLID dataset, are almost universally reported using accuracy or F1-macro at a single default decision threshold, on a single official train/test split, without significance testing across model comparisons and without regard to the asymmetric real-world cost of moderation errors. We re-evaluate five classifiers (Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) on TF-IDF features from OLID using Optuna-tuned hyperparameters, 50-fold repeated stratified cross-validation with Friedman/Nemenyi/Wilcoxon significance testing, and a nested (leakage-free) cost-optimal threshold search evaluated against the untouched official holdout test set across a range of FN:FP cost ratios (5:1 to 20:1) grounded in published content-moderation labor-cost figures. LightGBM achieves the best CV F1-macro (0.7115) and is statistically superior to Linear SVM, XGBoost, and Random Forest (Nemenyi p<0.002), but is not statistically distinguishable from Logistic Regression (p=0.354). Critically, threshold calibration alone reduces deployment cost by 30 to 79% relative to the naive 0.5 threshold across all five models, and the model ranking by deployment cost after calibration does not match the ranking by F1-macro: Linear SVM, the model with the smallest average CV advantage, becomes the cheapest model to deploy at low-to-moderate cost ratios, while LightGBM, the statistically best classifier, benefits least from calibration (31.8% average reduction versus 61.4% for Linear SVM). These results suggest that for cost-sensitive content moderation deployment, threshold selection is a more consequential design decision than model choice, and that model comparisons reported at a fixed 0.5 threshold can misrepresent which model is actually preferable in production

title: An Experimental Event-Driven Chess Algorithm Based on Structural Trajectories
abstract: This article presents both the structural chess algorithm and its direct implementation. The algorithm itself is operational: it can analyze a chess position, construct local structural gradients, generate candidate actions, examine their consequences, and adapt its trajectory after the opponent's response. However, in its untrained form, this mechanism is of limited practical value. The reason is not that the algorithm is unable to generate reasonable moves, but that the chess problem provides only a partial gradient. At a given structural level, many different actions and transitions may be locally consistent and individually justified, while only some of them remain useful when considered as part of a longer global trajectory. This issue is related to the author's earlier work on partial-gradient problems. The corresponding papers are available from the author's publication record and may be read, or even challenged, as a theoretical basis for the interpretation used here. The central point is that a partial gradient does not uniquely determine a global solution at the same level of representation. When several locally valid directions remain possible, additional structure is required to distinguish between them. Otherwise, the general alternative is effectively an expansion or enumeration of the possible transitions. For this reason, the present chess algorithm is designed to operate together with learned weights. These weights should not be confused with the conventional weights of a neural network. They do not represent a large distributed numerical model from which the move is directly inferred. In this implementation, a weight is attached primarily to an action, a structural transition, a response pattern, or a trajectory fragment. The memory therefore records which structural transitions tend to remain useful, which are quickly neutralized, which preserve the stability of the player's own position, and which successfully increase structural damage to the opponent. This distinction is important for both computational time and memory consumption. Instead of storing a large model describing every possible position, the system can retain a relatively small set of learned preferences over reusable structural transitions. The algorithm performs the structural analysis, while the memory gradually changes the probability and priority with which different transitions are explored. Thus, learning does not replace the algorithm; it makes the partial gradient navigable. In this sense, the untrained system can be simultaneously intelligent and ineffective: it may correctly identify many strong local possibilities while lacking sufficient information to distinguish the globally useful one. Training is therefore interpreted here not as teaching the rules of chess from the beginning, but as adjusting the weights of actions and transitions so that the existing structural mechanism progressively selects more persistent and globally coherent trajectories. The implementation accompanying this article is provided together with the article itself. It is intended to make the proposed mechanism directly testable: the same structural algorithm can be run without trained memory, trained through self-play, and then evaluated again using the accumulated transition weights.

title: Infectious Bovine Pinkeye Detection Using Computer Vision and Imbalance-Aware Learning
abstract: Infectious bovine pinkeye is a contagious ocular disease that adversely affects cattle health, welfare, and agricultural productivity. Conventional diagnosis relies primarily on clinical observation, which can be subjective, time-consuming, and difficult to implement efficiently in large herds or remote settings. This study evaluated and compared You Only Look Once (YOLO) v11 and YOLOv26 for automated bovine pinkeye classification and investigated the effects of class-balancing strategies on model performance. Five variants (n, s, m, l, and x) of each architecture were trained and evaluated using the original imbalanced dataset, Random Minority Oversampling (RMO), and an adapted Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE). Both YOLOv11 and YOLOv26 demonstrated strong classification performance, although the effects of class balancing varied across model variants. For YOLOv11, RMO-s achieved an accuracy of 0.99, a macro F1-score of 0.98, and a true positive rate (TPR) of 1.00, with no false-negative classifications. RMO-m also achieved a TPR of 1.00 with no false negatives. For YOLOv26, the original l, RMO-m, and RMO-l variants each achieved an accuracy of 0.99 and a macro F1-score of 0.98, with RMO-l attaining a TPR of 1.00 and no false negatives. Overall, RMO generally provided greater improvements in minority-class detection than adapted SMOTE, whereas the strong performance of the original YOLOv26-l demonstrates that oversampling was not necessary for all model variants. These findings demonstrate the potential of YOLOv11 and YOLOv26 for automated detection of bovine pinkeye and support further evaluation for livestock health monitoring.

title: Accurate Motion Estimation with Bézier Control Point for Efficient Frame Interpolation
abstract: In frame interpolation tasks, motion ambiguity in the training set causes models to generate blurry intermediate frames. Moreover, the assumption of uniform motion between frames during inference further leads to inaccuracies in the generated intermediate frames. To tackle these challenges, we propose an Accurate motion estimation algorithm with Bézier Control point, ABC-Inter, for efficient frame Interpolation. Specifically, ABC-Inter designs an Accurate Flow estimation Module (AFM) by decoupling two-frame features and mapping to corresponding coordinates to better estimate the optical flow between the two frames. Furthermore, ABC-Inter eliminates motion ambiguity in the training set by introducing Bézier control points that are computed using the input frames and the intermediate ground-truth (gt) frames. This allows the model to estimate accurate optical flow between two frames during the training process, thereby solving the blurriness problem in the generated intermediate frames during inference. Benefiting from the more accurate flow estimation between two frames, we can introduce additional frames and directly use multiple flows to calculate Bézier control points for modeling non-uniform motion without retraining the model. Simultaneously, to realize the estimation of non-linear motion using only two frames, we also introduce a new Bézier control point estimation module which achieves better motion estimation between the two frames by performing fine-tuning on the model in the second stage. Experimental results demonstrate that our ABC-Inter achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets and exhibits excellent visual perception.

evidence.abstract: In frame interpolation tasks, motion ambiguity in the training set causes models to generate blurry intermediate frames. Moreover, the assumption of uniform motion between frames during inference further leads to inaccuracies in the generated intermediate frames. To tackle these challenges, we propose an Accurate motion estimation algorithm with Bézier Control point, ABC-Inter, for efficient frame Interpolation. Specifically, ABC-Inter designs an Accurate Flow estimation Module (AFM) by decoupling two-frame features and mapping to corresponding coordinates to better estimate the optical flow between the two frames. Furthermore, ABC-Inter eliminates motion ambiguity in the training set by introducing Bézier control points that are computed using the input frames and the intermediate ground-truth (gt) frames. This allows the model to estimate accurate optical flow between two frames during the training process, thereby solving the blurriness problem in the generated intermediate frames during inference. Benefiting from the more accurate flow estimation between two frames, we can introduce additional frames and directly use multiple flows to calculate Bézier control points for modeling non-uniform motion without retraining the model. Simultaneously, to realize the estimation of non-linear motion using only two frames, we also introduce a new Bézier control point estimation module which achieves better motion estimation between the two frames by performing fine-tuning on the model in the second stage. Experimental results demonstrate that our ABC-Inter achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets and exhibits excellent visual perception.
